notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The consistency metric and the gap it exposes — τ-bench: a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • The judge's ceiling, when a rubric is the only available grade — Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv 2306.05685)

  • How practitioners scope an agent eval before writing one — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • why agent eval is uniquely hard — trajectories, non-determinism, compounding, many valid paths.

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — what the two metrics mean.

What this note adds: the commitment. "Agent eval is hard" is a description; the decision is which single number you'll be held to — and the arithmetic showing that the same agent scores 99.99% or 5.8% depending on which one you picked.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
pass@k vs pass^k, in one line? Succeeded at least once, versus succeeded every time.
Which one a user experiences? pass^k — they get one run, and then another.
What τ-bench showed? pass@1 under 50%, pass^8 under 25% for the same agent.
When you grade the end state? When the agent mutates things — the answer can lie, the world can't.
A judge's ceiling? Human agreement, around 80% — so ~20% disagreement is the floor.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I pick the grade before building the harness, because it decides everything downstream. If actions have side effects I grade the end state — did the refund exist, is the ticket closed — because the agent's own account of what it did is the least reliable evidence available. If there's a checkable answer I grade that. I only grade the path when the path is the requirement, as in a compliance flow, because otherwise a reference trajectory punishes the valid creative routes. And I commit to pass^k rather than pass@k, because the user gets one run: the same agent can read 99.99% on one metric and 5.8% on the other, and only one of those describes their experience.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Final answer A checkable ground truth exists. Blind to how it got there — a lucky path scores like a sound one. Question-shaped tasks with known answers.
End-state assertion The agent mutates real systems. The default when it acts. Needs a resettable world; says nothing about cost or path quality. Tools that write, send, refund or delete.
Trajectory against a reference The procedure is the requirement. Fails valid alternative routes; breaks whenever a tool changes. Regulated flows where the steps are auditable obligations.
Rubric judge over the trajectory Open-ended work with no ground truth. Judge cost, judge bias, and a ceiling at human agreement. Research, drafting, analysis.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Final answer A dataset of tasks with answers. Cheapest — one comparison per run. Scores move when the answer key ages, not when the agent does.
End state A resettable environment: fixtures, seeded data, teardown. Environment setup per trial dominates. The eval becomes infrastructure someone owns and keeps working.
Trajectory Reference paths stored and versioned with the tool catalogue. Cheap to run, expensive to maintain. Every tool rename is an eval migration.
Rubric judge A judge model, a rubric, and bias controls. A judge call per trajectory, on top of the run. Rubric drift, and a second model whose upgrades move your scores.

The redraw test lands on the end-state row: it's the only one that adds environment to the diagram rather than a comparison step. That's why teams default to final-answer grading for agents that act — it needs no infrastructure — and it's also why their eval keeps passing while production breaks.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The metric choice is worth more than any model upgrade. For a task with per-run success probability p, over k independent attempts:

pass@k = 1 − (1 − p)ᵏ        pass^k = pᵏ

At p = 0.7 and k = 8:

  • pass@8 = 1 − 0.3⁸ = 1 − 0.0000656 = 0.99993
  • pass^8 = 0.7⁸ = 0.0576

The same agent is 99.99% or 5.8%. Neither number is wrong; they answer different questions. pass@k asks "can it ever do this", which is the right question when a verifier picks the winning attempt — code generation against a test suite. pass^k asks "does it do this every time", which is the right question when a customer gets whatever the one run produced.

This is not hypothetical. τ-bench reports state-of-the-art agents succeeding on under 50% of tasks at pass@1, and under 25% at pass^8 in the retail domain. Roughly half the headline survives the requirement to be consistent across eight trials — so any agent number quoted without its k and its metric is uninterpretable.

How many trials you need to believe a difference. For a proportion, the standard error is √(p(1−p)/n). At p ≈ 0.72:

se = √(0.2016 / n)

To resolve a 5-point difference at roughly two standard errors, you need se ≈ 0.025, so n ≈ 0.2016 / 0.000625 ≈ 320 trials per arm. That's the honest cost of an end-to-end number you'd gate on, and it's why the cheap deterministic layers exist — not because they're better signals, but because 320 trials of a real trajectory is a budget line.

Why the agent's self-report is not a grade. An end-state assertion queries the system the agent was supposed to change. A final-answer grade reads what the agent says it did. Those diverge precisely in the interesting cases — the tool call that timed out after mutating state, the retry that double-charged, the action reported as done that silently failed validation. If the agent acts, the world is the ground truth and the transcript is a claim.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The metric branch hangs below the grading branch rather than beside it, because they're independent choices that get conflated. You can assert on the end state and still report pass@k, and that combination is how a rigorous-looking harness produces a number nobody's user will recognise.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The eval said 94% and support volume went up after launch."

Root cause. The harness graded the agent's final message against a reference answer, which is a reasonable choice for a question-answering system and the wrong one for this agent, which also updated records. In the failing cases the agent reported a successful update in its final message, the grader matched the reference text, and the record was never written — a tool call had returned a validation error the agent summarised as "done". The eval was measuring the agent's description of its work, and the agent was reliably good at writing that description.

Fix. The grade moved to an assertion against the database after the run, which required building a seeded, resettable fixture environment — about two weeks of work that had been skipped precisely because answer-matching needed none. The score dropped from 94% to 61% overnight, and that number was the first one that predicted production. Applying it late also meant the historical trend was worthless, because it had been measuring a different thing than everyone believed.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does the metric matter so much if the agent is the same agent?

Because the two metrics answer different questions and the gap between them widens with k. pass@k rewards the existence of a good run, which is genuinely the right frame when something downstream selects the winner — a test suite accepting one of eight candidate patches, say. pass^k rewards never failing, which is the frame when whatever the single run produced is what the customer receives.

The arithmetic makes the stakes concrete: at a 70% per-run success rate, eight attempts gives you 99.99% on one metric and 5.8% on the other. So a number quoted without its metric and its k isn't a weak claim, it's an uninterpretable one — and in a design round, asking which one someone means is usually the fastest way to find out whether they've measured anything.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

End-state assertions need a resettable environment. When is that not worth building?

When the agent doesn't act, which is rarer than people assume — a read-only research agent can legitimately be graded on its output. And in early exploration, where you're comparing prompts rather than deciding to ship, answer-matching moves fast enough to be useful and cheap enough to throw away.

What I'd refuse is carrying that choice into a gate. The moment a number blocks a release or appears in a plan, it has to be measuring the thing that can hurt you, and for an acting agent that's the state of the systems it touched. The fixture environment is real work, and the honest framing is that it's the cost of having an eval at all rather than an optional upgrade — an acting agent without a resettable world doesn't have a cheaper eval, it has a decorative one.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks in these grades as the task horizon gets longer?

pass^k collapses, and correctly so. Longer tasks mean more steps, more chances to fail, and a per-run success rate that falls — so the consistency metric drops faster than the single-attempt one, and a benchmark result on short tasks tells you very little about long ones.

Reference-trajectory grading breaks differently and worse: the space of valid paths grows combinatorially with horizon, so a fixed reference path fails an increasing share of correct runs. At any real length it's measuring conformity rather than success. That's the scaling argument for end-state assertions — the set of acceptable end states stays small even when the set of acceptable paths explodes.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the eval for an agent that processes refunds.

The grade is the end state: after the run, does a refund of the right amount exist against the right order, exactly once. That last clause is the one that catches the failure people miss, because a retried run that refunds twice passes any assertion written as "a refund exists".

The environment is a seeded ledger reset per trial, which also gives the idempotency check somewhere to live. I'd report pass^k with k around 5, since a customer gets one attempt and the risk is a rare double-refund rather than an occasional miss — and a metric that averages over attempts hides exactly that.

The part I'd raise unprompted is that this eval needs a second grade beside success: a harm count. A refund that doesn't happen is a support ticket; a duplicate refund is money gone, and those don't belong in the same number. Splitting the score into task success and harm rate is what lets you ship at 80% success, which you can never justify while a single figure is hiding the difference.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Our agent is at 90% on the eval."

✅ Reality: On which metric, at what k? At 70% per-run success, the same agent reads 99.99% at pass@8 and 5.8% at pass^8. A figure without its metric describes nothing.

❌ Trap: "We grade the final answer, which is what the user sees."

✅ Reality: For an acting agent the user also sees the consequences. The final message is the agent's claim about its work, and it's most confidently wrong exactly when a tool call half-failed.

❌ Trap: "We compare the trajectory to a golden path, so we catch wrong reasoning."

✅ Reality: You also fail every valid alternative route, and the count of those grows with task length. Reference paths measure conformity; use them where conformity is the requirement.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • why agent eval is uniquely hard — the properties this note commits to a number against.

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — the two metrics.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 Which layer you gate on, and which you only diagnose with — this is the grade the top layer uses.

  • §12 Recorded tool responses, a simulated world, or a live sandbox — an end-state grade demands a resettable world.

  • §1 Which metrics you commit to before drawing a single box — this is that commitment, made precise.

  • §8 Optimising for the best run or for every run — pass^k is that argument in metric form.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the refund design above is the whole eval story.

  • §14 Coding agent — the one place pass@k is genuinely the honest metric, because tests select the winner.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • How component and end-to-end evals are scoped in practice — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

  • The consistency gap that component scores hide — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • Running the layered stack against a real agent — LangSmith: evaluating a complex agent

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the granularities and what each tells you.

  • the 95% problem — why per-step success compounds multiplicatively.

What this note adds: the division of labour. Every layer is worth measuring and only one is worth gating on, and the reason is a cost asymmetry: the cheap layers are deterministic and the truthful layer needs hundreds of trials. Getting that backwards is why teams have four eval suites and still ship regressions.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What component scores can't tell you? Whether the task succeeds — errors compound across steps.
Per-step rate for 90% over 20 steps? 99.5%. Not a prompt fix.
Why the bottom layers exist? They're deterministic and cheap — fast signal, not truthful signal.
Which layer blocks a merge? Deterministic checks per commit; the top layer gates releases.
The trap? Green components composing into a failing task.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I run all four layers and gate on two of them at different cadences, because they differ in cost by two orders of magnitude. Tool-call validity and step success are deterministic — one run each, seconds, so they block every commit. End-to-end task success is the only honest number and it needs a few hundred trials to resolve a five-point move, so it gates releases rather than commits. The layers in between are diagnostics: they tell me where a regression happened once the top layer says one did. The trap I'd name before anyone asks is that high component scores don't imply task success — at 95% per step over twenty steps you're at 36%, and every component looks excellent.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Gate on component layers only Never, as the whole story. Blind to compounding and integration — passes while the task fails. All-green dashboards, rising escalations.
Gate on end-to-end only Small task set, slow release cadence. Hundreds of trials per gate; tells you that it broke, not where. One number, days to run, no diagnosis.
Deterministic per commit, end-to-end per release Anything shipping continuously. The default. Two cadences and two suites to maintain. Fast iteration plus a release bar.
Gate on a production canary Traffic is high and failures are recoverable. Real users meet the regression first. Offline tasks that never match production's mess.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Component gating A fixture per tool and per step. Seconds per commit. Fast feedback; false confidence when compounding does the damage.
End-to-end gating A task set, a resettable environment, a trial runner. Hundreds of runs — the dominant eval line. Slow, and the only signal that tracks what users get.
Both, split by cadence Both of the above, wired to different triggers. Cheap path per commit, expensive path per release. A diagnosis story: top layer fires, lower layers localise.
Canary gating Traffic splitting and an online metric with a rollback trigger. Almost free to run. An on-call story, and a blast radius per deploy.

The diagnostic chain is the part worth drawing: the end-to-end number tells you a release is worse, the trajectory layer tells you which step, the step layer tells you which tool, and the tool-call layer tells you whether the arguments were even valid. Without the lower layers you get a red gate and a week of bisecting; without the top one you get four green dashboards and an incident.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why component excellence doesn't survive composition. With independent per-step success s over n sequential steps, task success is sⁿ:

0.95²⁰ = 0.358

Twenty steps at 95% each — which would be an excellent component score on any dashboard — is a 36% task success rate. Nothing in the component layer is failing; the multiplication is.

Inverted, it explains why prompt work stops helping. For 90% end-to-end over 20 steps, the required per-step rate is:

s = 0.9^(1/20) = 0.9947

99.5% per step. That's not reachable by rewording an instruction, which is why the honest levers are the structural ones — fewer steps, or recovery so a step doesn't have to be right first time. The arithmetic is what turns "we'll improve the prompt" into a claim someone can check.

The cost asymmetry that decides the cadence. A deterministic check runs once: did the tool call parse, were the arguments in range, did the schema validate. An end-to-end number is a proportion, so its standard error is √(p(1−p)/n), and resolving a five-point change at p ≈ 0.72 takes roughly 320 trials per arm. One layer costs a second; the other costs hundreds of full agent runs. That ratio, not any principle about test pyramids, is why the split exists.

What the layers actually diagnose. Tool-call validity catches schema and argument bugs. Step success catches a tool returning something the agent can't use. Trajectory catches loops, wandering and premature stopping. End-to-end catches everything, attributes nothing. Each one is a filter on the layer above it, and the value of the stack is the attribution rather than the coverage — the top layer already covers everything.

Where independence fails, and why it matters. sⁿ assumes steps fail independently, and they don't: a bad retrieval at step three poisons every step after it, so real trajectories are worse than the formula in the tail and better in the middle, because agents sometimes recover. That's an argument for measuring end-to-end rather than computing it from component scores — the composition isn't multiplication, it's just also not free.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The drill-down is a terminal node rather than a loop back, because that's the moment the lower layers earn their existence. Everywhere else they're a fast smoke test; here they're the difference between naming the broken step in an hour and bisecting a release for a week.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Every eval was green and the new release resolved fewer tickets than the old one."

Root cause. The suite was three component evals: tool selection accuracy, argument validity, and retrieval relevance, each above 95% and each genuinely measuring what it claimed. The regression was in how the agent recovered — a prompt change had made it stop retrying after an ambiguous tool result, so runs that previously self-corrected at step four now terminated with a partial answer. No component was worse; the composition was. Nothing in the suite ran a full trajectory, so nothing could see it.

Fix. An end-to-end suite of 200 seeded tasks was added on release candidates, with the component evals kept per-commit for speed. The regression reproduced immediately and the trajectory layer localised it to early termination within an afternoon. The late cost was that the release had been out for nine days, and the ticket-resolution shortfall had already been absorbed as headcount by the support team — the eval gap had turned into a staffing decision before anyone traced it to a prompt.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

If end-to-end covers everything, why keep the lower layers at all?

For attribution and for speed, neither of which the top layer provides. End-to-end tells you a number moved; it can't tell you which of forty tool definitions or which prompt section caused it, so on its own it turns every regression into a bisect. The lower layers are a map from a red number to a place in the code.

Speed is the other half. A deterministic check runs in seconds and can sit on every commit, so most mistakes are caught by the author while they still remember the change. Running a few hundred full trajectories on every push isn't affordable and wouldn't be fast enough to be feedback if it were.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How do you set the threshold on the end-to-end gate?

Below the baseline's lower confidence bound, and derived rather than chosen. With 100 trials at 80% success, the 95% interval is roughly ±1.96 × √(0.16/100), about eight points — so a gate demanding "at least 80%" fails around half the time on an unchanged system, and the team learns to re-run it until it's green. At that point the gate is decoration with a cost.

Two ways out, and I'd take both. Raise n until the interval is tighter than the regression you care about, and compare paired rather than absolute — run baseline and candidate on the same tasks with the same seeds and test the paired difference, which cancels task difficulty and cuts the variance you're fighting. Paired comparison typically buys more resolution per trial than doubling the trial count does.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens to this stack when the task set grows to thousands of tasks?

The end-to-end gate stops being affordable per release, and the answer is stratified sampling rather than more compute. Partition the task set by the dimensions you actually care about — domain, difficulty, tools exercised — and sample within strata, so the gate runs a few hundred trials that represent the whole set instead of a few hundred that over-represent whatever's cheapest.

The second thing that breaks is staleness. A large task set accumulates tasks whose answers aged, whose tools were renamed, whose fixtures drifted, and those show up as regressions that aren't. At that size the suite needs its own maintenance budget and a flakiness metric per task, or you spend the gate's credibility on investigating your own rot.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the eval strategy for a coding agent.

Coding is the rare case where the top layer is both cheap and perfect, because the test suite is the grader — so end-to-end runs on every commit rather than per release, and the usual cost asymmetry doesn't apply. That inverts the normal advice and it's worth saying why: the expensive part of end-to-end eval is usually building a resettable world with a trustworthy verdict, and a repository with tests already is one.

So the layers I'd keep below it are the ones tests don't cover: did the agent read files it didn't need, how many steps did it take, what did it cost. Those aren't correctness, they're the efficiency and cost story from §10, and they regress silently because a passing test suite hides them.

The judgment call I'd flag is pass@k versus pass^k here. With tests selecting the winner, pass@k is genuinely the honest metric for a patch-generation workflow — and it stops being honest the moment the agent commits its own work without a human choosing between attempts. Which metric applies is a product decision about the workflow, not an eval-design one, and it's worth getting explicit before the number is quoted anywhere.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "All our component evals are above 95%, so the agent is reliable."

✅ Reality: 0.95²⁰ = 36%. Component scores multiply; the dashboard doesn't do the multiplication for you.

❌ Trap: "We'll improve the prompt to get end-to-end up."

✅ Reality: 90% over 20 steps needs 99.5% per step. Past a point the reachable levers are fewer steps or recovery, and saying which one you're pulling is the answer.

❌ Trap: "The gate is at the baseline score, so any regression fails it."

✅ Reality: At 100 trials and 80% success the noise is ±8 points, so it fails at random and gets re-run until green. Gate below the lower bound, or compare paired.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the layers this note assigns jobs to.

  • the 95% problem — the compounding that makes the top layer necessary.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 What counts as the score — the grade the top layer applies.

  • §12 What blocks the merge, and what only reports — the cadence this split implies.

  • §12 What a span must carry, and whose backend holds it — the drill-down only works if the trace recorded the step.

  • §8 Buy reliability with fewer steps or with verification gates — the two levers the per-step arithmetic leaves you.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — the one design where the top layer is cheap enough to gate every commit.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — long trajectories make the compounding arithmetic the headline.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The standard span shape, which is what makes the backend swappable — OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions

  • What an agent-native backend adds over generic tracing — Langfuse: observability SDK

  • The disclosure risk a content-bearing trace creates — OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • tracing & observability — spans, trace structure and the tooling landscape.

What this note adds: the contract. A trace is only worth its cost if it answers the questions you'll actually ask at 2am — which step failed, what did the tool really return, what was the model shown, what did it cost — and most traces can't, because they record the agent's summary instead of its inputs. Plus the buy/build fork the span standard makes reversible.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The test for a span? Can you replay the step from it alone.
The field most often missing? The tool's raw arguments and raw result.
Why cost belongs on the span? Per-step cost is where the steps² term becomes visible.
Why the standard matters commercially? A standard shape makes the backend replaceable.
What you must not sample? Anything that has to be evidence — that's the audit record.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The span contract comes before the vendor. A span has to let me replay the step without the agent's help: the exact model input, the tool name, the raw arguments, the raw result, the token counts and the cost, and the parent link so the trajectory reconstructs. Most traces store the model's narration of the tool result instead of the result, which is the one thing you can't trust when you're debugging. On the backend I start with an agent-native product for the trajectory views, and I emit under the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions so that choice stays reversible — the standard shape is the thing that stops observability from becoming a migration project.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Application logs only Never past a prototype. No trajectory, no parent links, no cost attribution. Debugging by grepping for a run id.
Generic OTel + existing backend You already run tracing and want one pane. Trajectory views you build yourself; no eval integration. A platform team with an opinion about telemetry.
Agent-native platform Iterating on prompts and evals. The default early. Vendor pricing, and your content in their store. Prompt and eval work is the daily job.
Both — native SDK, OTel wire format Once it matters. Slight duplication of config. You want the views now and the option later.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Logs only None. Free. Every incident is an archaeology exercise.
Generic OTel An exporter and a collector you already have. Storage by span volume. One pane, one retention policy — and trajectory views are yours to build.
Agent-native Their SDK in the request path; their store holds prompts and results. Per-trace or per-seat pricing. Prompt diffing, eval runs and trajectory replay out of the box.
Both Native SDK emitting OTel-shaped spans. Marginal. Backend becomes a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

The row that changes what you can do is the content one: a span carrying raw tool arguments and results turns debugging into replay, and turns your trace store into a system holding customer data. Both consequences follow from the same field, which is why the retention decision and the debuggability decision are the same decision.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The span contract, as a checklist you can test. A span for a step is sufficient if a person holding only that span can re-issue the call. That requires:

  • the model input actually sent, not the template
  • the tool name, the raw arguments, and the raw result
  • token counts split into input, output, cache-read and cache-creation
  • the computed cost, and the model and version that produced it
  • the parent span id, so the trajectory reconstructs

The field that decides debuggability is the raw tool result. If the trace stores the model's summary of what a tool returned, then in the failure you care about — the tool returned an error and the agent narrated success — the trace agrees with the agent and contradicts reality.

Why per-step cost belongs on the span, not in a monthly report. Cost per run is Σ over steps, and the growth term only becomes visible when you can see the input token count climbing step by step. A per-run total tells you a run was expensive; a per-span breakdown tells you it was expensive because the context was re-billed twenty times, which is a different fix. The four token fields are what make a cache-hit-rate regression show up as a graph rather than a surprise.

Sampling: the line between a trace and a record. Traces are sampled, and that's correct — full-fidelity tracing of every run at volume costs more than it's worth. What must never be sampled is anything that has to be evidence later: an approval, an effectful tool call, a policy decision. Those go to the append-only record on the write path. If the same pipeline carries both, you will discover the sampling rate during a dispute.

Retention, as two clocks rather than one. Spans carrying prompts and tool results concentrate personal data, so their clock is short — days to weeks. The record carrying identifiers and decisions is small and defensible to keep for years. Running one store at the longest retention means holding customer content for the duration of your compliance obligation, which is the expensive way to fail an audit.

The standard is the exit cost. Agent-native platforms are genuinely better at the daily work — trajectory diffing, prompt versioning, eval runs against traced data. The reason to emit under the GenAI semantic conventions anyway is that it makes the backend a routing decision. Bespoke instrumentation against one vendor's schema is a rewrite to leave; a standard span shape is a config change.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The contract question comes before the vendor question because no backend fixes a span that didn't record the tool's actual output. Teams reliably do this in the other order, buy a platform, and discover that the beautiful trajectory view is rendering the same narration their logs already had.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We had full tracing and still couldn't explain why the agent told a customer their order was cancelled."

Root cause. The instrumentation recorded, for each step, the model's message and the tool name — a reasonable-looking span that rendered nicely as a trajectory. It did not record what the tool returned. The cancellation tool had responded with a structured error the agent summarised as a success, and since the trace stored the summary, the trajectory view showed a clean successful cancellation. The trace and the agent agreed, and both were wrong, and there was no third source.

Fix. Raw tool arguments and results were added to the span, which immediately made the class of failure visible and also made the trace store hold order data — so retention dropped to fourteen days and the effectful calls were forked to the append-only record. Applying it late cost more than the instrumentation: the incident could not be scoped, because reconstructing which customers had been told something false meant querying the downstream system for cancellations that didn't exist rather than reading it from a trace.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

What makes an agent trace different from a normal distributed trace?

The shape is the same — spans, parents, durations — and the content isn't. A normal trace records that a call happened and how long it took, because the interesting questions are latency and errors. An agent trace has to record what the model was shown and what it produced, because the interesting question is why it decided something, and that decision is a function of its input text.

That pulls two things into the span a normal one omits: the actual prompt content, and token counts per call. The first is what makes the trace debuggable and also what makes it sensitive; the second is what makes cost attributable per step instead of per month.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Agent-native platform or your existing observability stack?

I'd take the agent-native platform early and the standard wire format always. Early on the daily work is prompt iteration, trajectory comparison and running evals against real traces, and a general-purpose backend does none of that — you'd spend months building views that a specialised product ships with.

What I wouldn't do is let that choice become structural. Emitting under the GenAI semantic conventions costs almost nothing at instrumentation time and means the backend is a destination rather than a dependency. The trap is the other order: bespoke SDK calls scattered through the agent, where switching backends means touching every call site, and the platform's pricing conversation happens with you holding no alternative.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks when trace volume grows a hundredfold?

Cost, first, and the reflex is to sample — which is right for traces and catastrophic if the same pipeline carries approvals and effectful calls. So the scaling event is what forces the split between the sampled trace and the unsampled record, and doing it before the volume arrives is much cheaper than during.

Second is content size. Agent spans carry prompts and tool results, so span payloads are kilobytes rather than bytes, and at high volume storage is dominated by text you'll read almost none of. Truncating large payloads with a pointer to object storage keeps the trajectory navigable and the bill sane — but the truncation rule has to preserve tool arguments and error bodies, which are small and are exactly what you need.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design observability for a multi-tenant agent platform.

Trace ids carry the tenant, and the trace store is namespaced per tenant rather than filtered by a predicate, for the same reason memory and caches are: a shared store with a tenant field leaks the first time someone writes a query without it, and support engineers write ad-hoc queries constantly.

Span content is the sensitive surface, so tenants get their own retention clock and their own deletion path — a deletion request has to be satisfiable against traces, which means traces are addressable by subject and not only by time. That requirement shapes the schema and is almost never designed in, because it only surfaces the first time someone exercises the right.

The part I'd raise unprompted is who gets to look. A shared internal dashboard over all tenants' trajectories is the most likely disclosure path in this design — not an attacker, an engineer debugging with a wide filter. So access is scoped and the access itself is logged, which is the same control the audit trail gets, applied to the people rather than the agent.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We trace every step, so we can debug anything."

✅ Reality: Only if the span holds the tool's raw result. If it holds the model's summary of that result, the trace corroborates the agent in exactly the failures where the agent is wrong.

❌ Trap: "Tracing and the audit trail are the same pipeline."

✅ Reality: Traces are sampled and expire by design. An approval that was sampled away isn't evidence. Same data shape, opposite requirements.

❌ Trap: "We'll pick the observability vendor later — it's just instrumentation."

✅ Reality: Instrumentation written against one vendor's schema is a rewrite to leave. Emitting the standard span shape makes it a config change, and costs nothing at the time.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • tracing & observability — the span model this note writes a contract for.

  • auditability and traceability — the record half of the split.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 Which layer you gate on — the drill-down is only possible if spans recorded the step.

  • §12 Which production signal you're willing to treat as a label — online labels attach to spans.

  • §11 Whether the audit trail is logging or a record of decision — the unsampled half, argued there.

  • §10 Which factor of the steps² term you attack — per-step token fields are how that becomes visible.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — trace namespacing and deletion are design constraints, not features.

  • §14 Deep research agent — long trajectories make parent links and per-step cost the only navigable view.

Absolute threshold versus paired comparison — when is absolute right?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Gating, thresholds and the flaky-eval problem, end to end — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

  • Why a benchmark number moves when you re-run it — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • Running evals against traced production data rather than a static set — LangSmith: evaluation

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Evals in CI — Gating, Thresholds & Flaky Evals — the tiered-suite pattern and why thresholds sit below the baseline.

  • Statistical Rigor in Evals — Error Bars & Paired Tests — error bars and paired comparison.

What this note adds: the trigger list and the failure mode. The interesting question isn't whether to run evals in CI, it's which changes trip which suite — a model version bump and a tool rename break different things — and what happens to a team when the gate is noisier than the regression it guards.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What trips the expensive suite? Model, prompt, tool schema or graph change — not every commit.
Where the threshold goes? Below the baseline's lower confidence bound.
Cheapest resolution gain? Paired comparison — same tasks, same seeds, test the difference.
The gate that's worse than none? One re-run until green; it manufactures consent.
What a model bump needs? The full suite — nothing about it is a local change.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I tier by what changed rather than by how often people commit. Deterministic checks — schemas, argument validity, refusal behaviour — run on every commit in seconds. The expensive trajectory suite runs on the four changes that can actually move behaviour globally: the model version, the system prompt, a tool schema, or the graph. Everything else gets the nightly run. The threshold is derived from the baseline's confidence interval rather than picked, because a gate that fails on noise gets re-run until it's green, and at that point it isn't a control — it's a log entry that says a human approved something.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Nothing blocks — nightly report Prototype, one owner. Regressions ship and are found by users. A dashboard nobody opens before merging.
Deterministic per commit only Fast iteration, low stakes. Blind to behaviour changes that still parse. Schema-valid output that answers worse.
Tiered by change type Anything shipping continuously. The default. Two suites, and a mapping from change to trigger. A model bump and a copy fix costing the same to merge.
Full suite on every commit Rare, tiny task sets. Slow merges; teams route around it. A queue of PRs waiting on evals.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Nightly only A scheduled job. Cheapest. Attribution is a day of commits wide.
Deterministic per commit Fast checks in the PR pipeline. Seconds. Authors fix their own mistakes while they remember them.
Tiered by change type Path-based triggers: prompt files, tool schemas, model config. Expensive suite runs rarely and deliberately. Changing a prompt becomes a reviewed event with a number attached.
Every commit One pipeline. Hundreds of runs per push. Merge latency, and pressure to weaken the gate.

The tiered row is the only one that adds something conceptual rather than a job: a declared mapping from kinds of change to kinds of risk. That mapping is the artefact — without it, the tiering is just a slower job on a cron, and the first time someone bumps a model in a config file nothing expensive runs.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why an obvious threshold fails constantly. A gate on a proportion inherits the proportion's noise. With n trials at success rate p, the 95% interval half-width is roughly:

1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n)

At p = 0.8 and n = 100: 1.96 × √(0.0016) = 1.96 × 0.04 = 0.078 — ±7.8 points. So a gate demanding "at least 80%" against an 80% baseline goes red roughly half the time on a system that didn't change. The team re-runs it, it passes, and within a month re-running until green is the workflow. The gate now produces a green tick on releases nobody evaluated, which is worse than no gate because it looks like evidence.

Two fixes, and the cheaper one isn't more trials. Raising n shrinks the interval as 1/√n, so halving the noise costs four times the compute. Paired comparison is the better lever: run baseline and candidate over the same tasks with the same seeds and test the paired differences. Task difficulty is the dominant variance component and it cancels exactly, so the same trial budget resolves a much smaller change. Absolute thresholds are for dashboards; gates should compare against the thing they're replacing.

What the trigger mapping should be. Four changes can move behaviour on tasks they don't mention, and they're the ones that warrant the expensive suite:

  • model version — everything, including tool-calling format adherence
  • system prompt — global, and the effects are rarely where you edited
  • tool schema or description — selection changes for tools you didn't touch
  • graph or control flow — recovery and termination behaviour

Anything else — a copy string, a log line, a retry constant — gets the deterministic checks and the nightly run. The point of naming the four is that they're the changes where a reviewer's intuition about blast radius is reliably wrong.

Flakiness needs its own number. A task that fails intermittently on an unchanged system is noise wearing a regression's clothes. Tracking per-task flip rate over nightly runs lets you quarantine the unstable ones out of the gate and into the report, so the gate's variance is the variance of tasks that actually behave. Without it, the suite's noise floor rises silently as it grows, and the threshold you derived last quarter stops holding.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The quarantine branch exists because the alternative is deleting flaky tasks, and flaky tasks are often the most informative ones — a task that passes 60% of the time is telling you something real about consistency. Moving it out of the gate and into the report keeps the signal without letting it spend the gate's credibility.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The eval gate had been green for six weeks. Then we found it had been running against the old model the whole time."

Root cause. The suite was triggered by changes under the prompts directory, which covered the case everyone had in mind when it was set up. The model id lived in a deployment config in a different repository, so a version bump — the single change with the widest blast radius — matched no trigger and ran nothing. The gate was green because it hadn't run, and a green tick and an unrun suite are indistinguishable in the pipeline UI.

Fix. Triggers moved from paths to a declared list of behaviour-affecting inputs, with the model id among them, and the pipeline began failing when the expensive suite hadn't run against the current configuration — so "not run" stopped rendering as "passed". The late cost was that six weeks of releases had no eval coverage, and re-establishing a baseline meant a full suite run against every intermediate version to find where the regression that users had been reporting had actually entered.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why not just run the full suite on everything and stop reasoning about triggers?

Cost and latency, and the second is the one that kills it. A few hundred trajectories per push means merge times measured in hours, and teams respond to that by batching changes, merging around the gate, or lowering the trial count until it's fast and meaningless. A control people route around isn't stricter than a tiered one, it's absent.

There's also a signal argument. Running the expensive suite on a log-message change adds a noisy measurement with nothing to attribute it to, so every false red costs credibility. Reserving it for the four changes that can genuinely move global behaviour means a red result is informative when it happens.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Absolute threshold versus paired comparison — when is absolute right?

Absolute is right for a release bar you've promised someone: this agent resolves at least 70% of tickets, and if it doesn't we don't ship. That's a product commitment and it needs an absolute number with enough trials behind it to be defensible.

For catching regressions, paired wins on every axis. You're not asking "is it good enough", you're asking "is it worse than what's running", and that's a comparison the paired design answers with far less compute because task difficulty cancels. I'd run both at different moments — paired on every trigger to catch regressions, absolute occasionally against the product bar to confirm the whole thing hasn't drifted somewhere the paired test can't see, since a slow decline that never shows a significant per-release step is exactly what paired testing misses.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens to this as the team grows to ten people merging daily?

Contention on the expensive suite, and then queueing. Ten people touching prompts means the trigger fires often, runs take an hour, and either they serialise or they run concurrently against the same fixtures and interfere. The usual resolutions are batching the expensive suite on a merge queue rather than per PR, and making the fixture environment per-run rather than shared.

The subtler failure is baseline drift. With a paired design, the baseline is whatever is currently on main, so a sequence of individually-insignificant regressions each passes its gate while the absolute number declines. That's the drift I'd want the occasional absolute run to catch, and it's an argument for a fixed reference version that the suite also compares against monthly rather than only comparing to yesterday.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the CI eval strategy for a platform where tenants write their own prompts.

The trigger mapping inverts: my model, my graph and my tool schemas are versioned by me and gate my releases, but tenant prompts change constantly and I can't run a trajectory suite per tenant edit. So tenants get the deterministic layer synchronously — schema validity, refusal behaviour, required tool presence — and that's what blocks their save.

Behavioural quality for tenants becomes an offline report they can run against their own task set, which means the eval harness is a product surface rather than internal tooling. That's a significant scope realisation and it's the sort of thing worth naming early, because it changes who builds it.

For platform changes, the bar goes up rather than down: a model version bump now affects every tenant's prompts, none of which I've seen. So the platform suite needs a corpus sampled across tenants — with consent and with content controls — because my own task set can't represent prompts I didn't write. That corpus question, not the pipeline, is the hard part of this design.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The gate is set at the baseline score, so any regression fails it."

✅ Reality: At 100 trials and 80% success the interval is ±7.8 points, so it fails at random. Within a month the team re-runs until green and the gate certifies releases nobody evaluated.

❌ Trap: "More trials is how you fix a noisy gate."

✅ Reality: Noise falls as 1/√n, so halving it costs 4× the compute. Pairing on the same tasks and seeds cancels task difficulty and buys more resolution for the same budget.

❌ Trap: "Evals run in CI, so changes are covered."

✅ Reality: Only the changes that match a trigger. A model id in a deployment config is the widest-blast-radius change there is, and it matches no path under prompts/.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Evals in CI — Gating, Thresholds & Flaky Evals — the tiered pattern this note assigns triggers to.

  • Statistical Rigor in Evals — Error Bars & Paired Tests — the statistics behind the threshold.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 Which layer you gate on — this note sets the cadence that split implies.

  • §12 Recorded tool responses, a simulated world, or a live sandbox — a per-commit suite needs a deterministic environment.

  • §12 When a judge earns its call — a judge in the gate adds its own variance to the threshold.

  • §13 Versioning — the model id being a gated input is a deployment-versioning decision.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — tests make the expensive suite cheap enough to gate every commit.

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — the tenant-prompt inversion above is the design.

notes.title: When a judge earns its call, and what you control for

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The named biases and the agreement ceiling — Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv 2306.05685)

  • Applying a judge to a trajectory rather than a single answer — LangSmith: trajectory evals

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • llm-as-judge for trajectories — how judges work and the known failure modes.

What this note adds: the eligibility rule and the ceiling. A judge is what you reach for when nothing decidable exists — and it can never be more reliable than the humans it imitates, which bounds what you're allowed to gate on it.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
When a judge is wrong to use? When a deterministic check would answer the same question.
The ceiling? ~80% agreement with humans — the same as human–human.
The three biases to control? Position, verbosity, self-enhancement.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A judge is the last resort, not the default. If the question is decidable — does it parse, does the cited id exist, did the refund land, is the amount right — that's code, and code doesn't have a bias table. I bring in a judge only for what genuinely has no ground truth: was the reasoning sound, was the tone right, did the research cover the question. And I hold it to what it is: strong judges reach about 80% agreement with human raters, which is roughly what humans reach with each other, so a judge's verdict carries a floor of about one disagreement in five. That bounds the size of the difference I'll let it gate.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Programmatic check The question is decidable. Always first. Only covers what you can express. Schemas, ids, amounts, end states.
Judge with a rubric Open-ended quality, no ground truth. A call per trajectory, ~20% disagreement floor, and bias controls. Research, drafting, explanation quality.
Judge with a reference answer Ground truth exists but is phrased many ways. Cheaper and steadier than open rubric; needs the references. Paraphrase-tolerant Q&A.
Human raters Calibrating the judge, or the stakes justify it. Slow and expensive; their own ~80% agreement. Establishing the baseline the judge is checked against.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Programmatic An assertion in the harness. Free. Deterministic — the same run scores the same twice.
Rubric judge A judge model, a versioned rubric, bias controls. A judge call per trajectory, often on a long transcript. The judge's own model upgrades move your scores.
Reference judge A reference set to maintain. Similar per call, lower variance. References age with the product.
Human raters A labelling workflow. The expensive one. The calibration set everything else is measured against.

The three controls, and what each costs. Position — when comparing two trajectories, run both orders and keep only consistent verdicts; this doubles judge cost and is the single highest-value control. Verbosity — judges favour longer answers, so either normalise length in the rubric or compare like-length candidates. Self-enhancement — a model prefers its own output, so the judge should not be the model under test, and when you upgrade the agent's model you should check whether the judge's relative scores moved.

What the ceiling means for gating. If the judge agrees with humans about 80% of the time, then roughly a fifth of its verdicts would be disputed by the people whose judgement it stands in for. A gate on a two-point judge difference is reading noise from a disagreeing rater. A judge is for catching large moves and ranking candidates, and the honest way to use one in a gate is to require the difference to exceed the judge's own measured disagreement rate on your task set — which means measuring that first.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Judge scores jumped four points the week we upgraded the agent's model, and human reviewers saw no difference."

Root cause. The judge and the agent were the same model family, and the upgrade landed on both — the eval pipeline pinned "latest". Self-enhancement bias did the rest: the new judge preferred the new agent's phrasing. Nothing about answer quality had changed, and the four points were a measurement artefact that a quarterly review had already recorded as progress.

Fix. The judge was pinned to a specific version and changed only deliberately, with a re-calibration run against the human-labelled set whenever it moved. The judge model was also chosen from a different family than the agent's. The late cost was that a quarter of reported improvements had to be re-derived, because nobody could tell which had been real and which had been the judge agreeing with itself.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • llm-as-judge for trajectories — the mechanism and its failure modes.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 What counts as the score — the judge is the fourth grade there, and the last resort.

  • §12 What blocks the merge — a judge in the gate adds its disagreement rate to the threshold.

  • §11 Which rails you build — the same "decidable in code first" rule, applied to safety.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — no ground truth, so the judge is the grade and its controls are the design.

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • A benchmark built on a simulated user and a rule-bound domain — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • Forking a run from a recorded state — LangGraph: time travel

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • simulation & replay — recorded responses, simulated users and sandboxed environments.

What this note adds: the fidelity–determinism trade, priced. Each option buys reproducibility with realism, and the choice is really about what kind of regression you're trying to catch — a prompt regression and an integration regression need opposite environments.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What recorded fixtures can't catch? Anything caused by a real tool changing behaviour.
What a live sandbox costs? Determinism — and the runs are slow and rate-limited.
What a simulated user adds? Multi-turn behaviour a fixture can't script.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I match the environment to the regression. Recorded tool responses are perfectly reproducible, so they're right for per-commit checks where the question is "did my prompt change break something" — the tools are held still on purpose. A live sandbox is the only thing that catches integration drift, so it runs nightly and slowly, and its failures are read as signals rather than gates because it isn't reproducible. A simulated user sits in between and is the only option when the task is a conversation, because a fixture can't respond to what the agent actually asked. Most teams pick one; the useful answer is that they catch different things.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Recorded responses Per-commit determinism. The default for fast checks. Blind to real tool changes; fixtures go stale silently. Prompt and graph iteration.
Simulated environment Multi-turn tasks, or a world with rules. A simulator to build and keep honest. The user is part of the task.
Live sandbox Catching integration drift before production does. Non-deterministic, slow, rate-limited, needs reset. Tools owned by other teams.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Recorded A fixture store keyed by call signature. Free to run. Fixtures need re-recording, and nothing tells you when.
Simulated A simulator with its own rules and its own bugs. Model calls for the simulated user. You now maintain two systems that can disagree.
Live sandbox A resettable deployment of real dependencies. Slow runs, real quota. Failures need triage — was it the agent or the dependency.

The staleness problem, which is the one that bites. A recorded fixture keeps passing after the real tool changed its response shape, so the suite is green while production breaks. The mitigation is cheap and almost never done: re-record periodically against the live sandbox and fail the build when a recorded response no longer matches what the real tool returns. That turns the fixture store from a snapshot into a contract test.

Why replay isn't the same as re-running. Replaying a recorded trajectory tests your grader and your analysis, not your agent — the decisions are already made. Forking from a checkpoint at step N and letting the agent decide again is the useful version, because it isolates one decision point while holding everything before it fixed. That's the cheapest way to ask "would the new prompt have recovered here", and it's a different mechanism from replaying a transcript.

The simulated user is a model, so it has variance too. A simulated user makes multi-turn eval possible and adds a second source of non-determinism — two runs diverge because the user behaved differently, not because the agent did. Pinning the user's model and seed, and keeping its persona short and scripted, is what keeps the trajectory attributable to the agent.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "CI was green for a month while the agent had been failing in production the whole time."

Root cause. Every eval ran against recorded tool responses, which is exactly what made CI fast and reproducible. A downstream team had changed an error response from a structured object to a plain string — a reasonable change they announced — and the agent's parsing broke. The fixtures still returned the old shape, so the suite kept exercising a version of the world that no longer existed, and did so confidently.

Fix. A nightly job re-recorded fixtures against the sandbox and failed when a response's shape had drifted, which converted a silent staleness problem into a loud one. Applying it late cost a month of degraded production behaviour, and the more expensive lesson was organisational: the announcement had been made, and nothing in the eval system was capable of reacting to it.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • simulation & replay — the three environments.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 What counts as the score — an end-state grade needs a resettable world, which is this decision.

  • §12 What blocks the merge — only the deterministic environment can gate a commit.

  • §7 Whether to support forking a run from step N — the same checkpoint machinery, used for eval.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — a simulated user is the only way to eval the conversation.

notes.title: Which production signal you're willing to treat as a label

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Running evaluation against production traces rather than a static set — LangSmith: evaluation

  • Why human corrections are the most informative feedback shape — Hugging Face: illustrating RLHF

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • human feedback loops & online eval — feedback loops and online evaluation.

What this note adds: the ranking. Production emits several candidate labels and they differ enormously in density and bias — the best one is usually the human edit, because it's a correction rather than an opinion, and it arrives from users who never click a thumb.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Best free label? The human edit — dense, and it says what right looked like.
Why thumbs are weak? Sparse and skewed to the annoyed and the delighted.
What escalation rate measures? Failure, without saying which step caused it.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I rank production signals by how much they tell me per unit of bias. Human edits are the best: if someone takes the agent's draft and changes it before sending, that's a dense, unsolicited label that also contains the correct answer — the diff is the training signal. Escalation rate is next, because it's unambiguous about failure even though it can't localise it. Explicit thumbs are last: sparse, and collected almost entirely from people who were annoyed or delighted. The pivot is that online labels are the only ones that reflect real traffic, so the offline suite should be fed from them rather than from what someone imagined users would ask.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Human edits as labels A human reviews output before it's used. The richest signal. Only exists where a review step does. Draft-then-send, or suggest-then-apply workflows.
Escalation / handoff rate The agent can hand off to a person. Says it failed, not where. A support or triage flow with a human fallback.
Downstream outcome The task has a later business result. Delayed, and confounded by everything else. Resolution, conversion, retention.
Explicit thumbs Nothing better exists. Sparse and polarised; unrepresentative of typical runs. A chat surface with no review step.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Edits Capture the before and after, joined to the trace. Free — the work was happening anyway. A stream of corrections that feeds the offline set.
Escalation A handoff event joined to the run. Free. A headline metric leadership already understands.
Downstream outcome An attribution join over days or weeks. Analysis work. The closest thing to business truth, and the slowest.
Thumbs A widget and a store. Cheap. A number that moves with mood; easy to over-read.

Why the edit is the strongest label. A thumb is an opinion with one bit of information. An edit is a correction: it says the output was wrong and what right would have been, at the granularity of the change. Collected at scale, edits are a labelled dataset for exactly the distribution your users produce, and their density is orders of magnitude above voluntary feedback because the human was going to do the work regardless.

The bias each one carries. Edits over-represent workflows with a review step, so they say nothing about unattended runs. Escalation under-counts silent failures, where a wrong answer was accepted. Downstream outcomes are confounded by everything else that happened. Thumbs skew to the extremes. None is unbiased, and naming the bias is what separates using a signal from being fooled by one.

The loop that makes this worth building. Online signals are only half useful as a dashboard; their real value is feeding the offline suite. A production run that was edited, escalated or thumbed down is a candidate task for the eval set, already carrying its own label. That's how a task set stays representative as usage drifts — otherwise it slowly becomes a record of what the team imagined at launch.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Thumbs-up rate was 94% and churn was rising."

Root cause. Feedback was collected from a widget under each answer, and roughly one run in two hundred produced a click. The people clicking were overwhelmingly those the agent had delighted; users whom it had wasted five minutes of simply left, and leaving emitted nothing. The metric measured enthusiasm among the enthusiastic, and it was being reported as satisfaction.

Fix. The headline moved to abandonment and escalation — runs with no accepted output, and runs handed to a human — both derived from behaviour rather than from volunteering. Thumbs stayed as a weak secondary. The late cost was two quarters of roadmap prioritised against a number that had never represented the users who mattered, and rebuilding the offline eval set from escalated traces rather than from the original hand-written tasks.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • human feedback loops & online eval — the feedback mechanisms.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 What a span must carry — labels attach to traces, so the join has to exist.

  • §12 Which layer you gate on — online signals keep the offline task set representative.

  • §1 Which metrics you commit to before drawing a single box — escalation rate is usually one of them.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — escalation rate is the metric the business already tracks.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The one that made consistency a headline metric — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • Real repository tasks with tests as the grader — SWE-bench (arXiv 2310.06770)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • agent benchmarks — what SWE-bench, τ-bench, GAIA and WebArena each measure.

What this note adds: what to do with the numbers. They rank models on someone else's distribution, which makes them a shortlist tool and never a readiness claim about your system.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What they're good for? Shortlisting models before you spend on your own eval.
What they don't predict? Your tools, your domain, your task length.
The number worth quoting? τ-bench's pass^8 — consistency, not a single attempt.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I use them to narrow a model shortlist and never to claim readiness. They measure a fixed distribution with someone else's tools, and the thing that determines whether my agent works is my tool schemas, my domain rules and my task lengths — none of which appear. The number I'd actually quote from one is τ-bench's consistency result, because it makes the general point that agent numbers collapse when you require the same task to succeed repeatedly: under 50% at a single attempt, under 25% across eight. That framing transfers to my system even though the score doesn't.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Shortlist models with them Choosing which two models to evaluate properly. The useful mode. Little — as long as the shortlist is then tested on your tasks. A model choice to make and no data yet.
Quote them as readiness Never. Credibility, the first time someone asks about your domain. A launch deck citing a leaderboard.
Build your own in that style The benchmark's shape fits your domain. Real work — tasks, graders, a resettable world. Your tasks look like τ-bench's but with your rules.
